newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hospitals hit as strikes sweep South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Hospitals hit as strikes sweep South Korea.

text.p: South Korean hospital workers walked out on strike on Friday, leaving only emergency care, as industrial action in protest at a new labour law spread from factories and shipyards to key services.
Nurses and orderlies closed out-patient sections of 14 hospitals, including Seoul National University Hospital, the country's leading medical centre.

A general strike loomed after the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the biggest umbrella labour group, called out its 1.2 million members for an initial 24-hour action from 1 p.m. (0400 GMT) on Friday.

The leading employers' group sought to calm workers by promising that controversial provisions of the new law allowing layoffs and flexible working hours would be used only as a last resort by struggling companies.
The law was railroaded through parliament on Thursday.

Layoffs would only occur if firms were in "extreme difficulties" and flexible working hours would not result in a loss in pay, the Korea Employers Federation pledged in a statement. Workers were urged to return to their jobs "because companies are suffering and the economy is not doing too well".
The law gives employers the right to replace striking workers. But federation official Ko Song-nam indicated that member companies would not seek to use this provision to break the current strikes.
"If the strikes go on, it is possible that there will be suspensions," he said by telephone. "Only in extreme cases will we close factories or use substitute workers".

Some 150,000 workers from the half million-strong Korea Confederation of Trade Unions responded to a call from their leaders to down tools on Thursday, halting production at South Korea's largest car plant, Hyundai Motor, and major shipyards.
Daewoo Group's shipyard was idled on Friday and workers at Daewoo car plants were set to join the stoppages.
Vehicle and ship production in South Korea is now virtually halted. Cars and ships are among the country's top exports.

Journalists joined protests against the labour bill, staging sit-down demonstrations late on Thursday at the union offices of the Korea Broadcasting System. Broadcast unions were due to meet on Friday to decide on strike action.
The government declared the strikes illegal, but although it has threatened "stern countermeasures" there was no sign yet of any crackdown on organised labour.
Huge worker rallies were planned on Friday on a concrete plaza near Seoul's new financial centre.
Economists fear the strikes could drag on until well into next year, threatening already feeble corporate profits.

Export earnings have been savaged this year by plunging international prices for South Korea's key products. Stockpiles are now high, but protracted strikes could run them down and eventually exacerbate a ballooning trade deficit.
Seoul subway workers voted to strike from Saturday, a half day for most workers, threatening transport chaos for tens of thousands of commuters in the capital.

Opposition members of parliament staged an overnight sit-down protest against the government's tactics in ramming through the labour law and another controversial law boosting the powers of the once-notorious domestic spy agency.
They vowed to occupy the chamber until midnight on Saturday.
The bills were passed at a dawn session on Thursday of the National Assembly attended only by ruling New Korea Party members.
